chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Union strictness then versus lax enforcement now
summary: Horace recalls strict officials and tax payments on one-nighters, versus today's local agents who barely check; a band at his current job never filed a contract.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Huh. How was it in those times, again '20's and '30's especially, in working with unions? I know you've mentioned a couple of times various things that have happened, but in general did you feel as much pressure from union or did you feel that the union was very useful or just how was it or did you just basically, ignore it?

Tom, I think in those days, in the early days, the union officials were more strict than they are now. I really do. I'm judging from the international -- of course, they've changed a lot, "and" and their personnel, of course. And Mr. Stanley Ballard, who was located in New Jersey, 220 Pleasant Avenue -- remember that?

That was an address that he occupied for years and years. He's just retired recently, but like you'd play one nighters, you'd have to send your tax in, and -- plus the fact that, when you had a big band, and you'd frequently the larger cities, there would be these business agents which actually see if you belong to the union, and if your dues -- if your card was up, we'd say, you know, and your dues were paid, and all those things. And a lot of people would collect the local tax at that time. But now you play a lot of dates, man, sometimes you'd be on a job three, four, five weeks before you even --

-- see the agent, and he doesn't even show up. He reads the newspapers, you know, like in the surrounding towns here. And say that you would get a letter from this particular guy in the jurisdiction that you play in, I'm from local so and so's secretary -- I see by the papers that you're playing the so and so. They're not as strict.

In fact a job that I'm closing on tonight, the band that played there before me was there for six months, and I met the guys when I first opened there, and they were union. They said -- I asked them, I said, 'What's the tax on this -- it's a different --

Yeah, it's Boulder Local, and I said, "Do you know the amount of tax?" They said, "Well, we've been here for six months, and we haven't paid any tax. We haven't -- I said, "Did you file your contract?" No, we didn't file a contract." Well, man, I could picture back in the old days, and they never did, but I was there, played for one week, and I got a letter.
And so I don't know what caused this thing, but there's a lot of negligence, like you have in Denver. I don't want to talk too much because I still live here, but it's a fact.

I have -- we do have a new administration here now in our local, and they're doing a very good job. And there were some discrepancies back a few years back. They're trying to rectify these things, but I think back in the days that you talked about the union -- the unions, I should say, were more helpful, I think, to the musicians because a lot of times, you know, the booking agents would have to file the contracts before the band entered that jurisdiction, and a lot of times the promoters would have to put up half the amount of the contract, you know, and then the business agent would come out and help you collect, you know. That doesn't happen now, you

know, so unfortunately, it's bad for the musician.
And in those days, as you know, the bands used to move around far more from what they do now, you know, like the one nighters, and they would be four, 500 miles apart, one of those things. In fact, those days you'd be happy to know that there were some union officials around, so you felt more or less protected.
